World.title: 11 years after decriminalisation, ganja use complicating mental health care
World.content:
AI image of a young man smoking marijuana. (Adobe stock)

Eleven years after Jamaica decriminalised ganja, the use of the substance features heavily among patients presenting with psychosis and schizophrenia. While there is currently no data establishing whether use of the herb is causing or contributing to the mental health problems, its prevalence is complicating treatment.

This is against the background of data from the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) pointing to an increase in high-risk usage of cannabis and the potency of the substance in Jamaica, as well as an increase in admissions for psychosis and schizophrenia over the last decade.

“What we do know is that the majority of psychiatric admissions in our public hospitals are coming from psychosis or schizophrenia. And the majority of those persons do use cannabis. So, we can look at that relationship and see that it is strong,” said Director for Treatment Services at the NCDA, Dr Kristen Robinson Barrett.

Still, Robinson Barrett noted that there is little data specifically exploring cannabis-induced psychosis.

Psychiatrist at Bellevue Hospital, Dr Brian Kazaara concurred that cannabis use has a striking presence among patients presenting with mental issues, but suggested that the substance rarely causes psychotic disorders.

“We don’t have official studies performed at Bellevue Hospital regarding cannabis use among patients, but from a cursory observation I can safely say the vast majority of patients admitted to the hospital also use cannabis,” he said.

Kazaara, who previously worked at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), pointed to a survey carried out by UHWI that revealed that the majority of persons admitted to the institution’s psychiatric ward smoked cannabis.

“What studies show is that persons with common psychiatric conditions like major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders use cannabis far more frequently than persons who do not have mental illnesses,” he said.

Despite this, Kazaara explained, “Cannabis-induced psychosis is not the norm. It is rare. At Bellevue we very, very rarely see that diagnosis. I also worked at UHWI for seven years [and] rarely saw it, almost never.”

Cannabis is a psychoactive drug and can affect the way that people perceive the world, leading to relaxation, paranoia, or other effects.

“It binds to our cannabinoid receptors around our body, but particularly in our brain, and that’s how we get the effects. It tends to create effects as it relates to emotions and feelings,” Robinson Barrett said. “They might experience changes as it relates to their time perception, so things might feel slowed down… issues with their concentration, so their attention and their awareness, their reaction time will change.”

Kazaara cautions that cannabis use can muddle the treatment of mental health issues.

“Cannabis definitely complicates psychosis, because for persons who use cannabis, they are more likely to develop an earlier onset of psychosis. So it may happen earlier than if they didn’t use it. It makes symptoms worse. It makes it harder to treat,” he explained.

Jamaica has a strong culture of recreational cannabis use, and Research Analyst at the NCDA Uki Atkinson explained that while overall population use has not necessarily changed over the last decade following decriminalisation of the drug, the potential for high-risk use has.

She supported her assessment with results from the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (CAST) which was used during surveys in 2016 and 2023.

“We were able to compare the levels of high-risk use from 2016 to 2023. In 2016, 50 per cent of the people who used cannabis in the past year were deemed to be at high risk for misusing it,” Atkinson said, noting “this has increased by 16 per cent in 2023. So, it shows not necessarily that more people are using ganja… But there’s a significant increase in high-risk patterns of use.”

In addition to high-risk usage, the potency of cannabis being consumed in Jamaica is also a concern.

According to a European study, using high-potency cannabis with a tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration over 10 percent, significantly increases the risk of developing psychotic symptoms or disorders, especially with daily use.

Robinson Barrett expressed serious concern about current potency trends worldwide compared to a potency of around four per cent in the 1990s.

“As of 2024, we’re looking at potencies of 15 to 20 per cent,” Robinson Barrett indicated.

“The potency trends of cannabis in Jamaica measured between 2014 and 2020, were showing that over that decade, the cannabis potency would have moved from about one per cent to over 10 per cent across 12 parishes,” she continued. “So, we’re concerned… because we have a culture of heavy use in young age groups…it’s a very concerning picture as it relates to all young people and any other vulnerable group.”

Outside of general risks, Robinson Barrett noted that there are some who may be particularly susceptible to the effects of cannabis use, including youth.

“Generally speaking, the earlier the age of onset for any substance is going to increase your risk for addiction, and it’s going to increase your risk for its effects…for the cannabis, we’re looking at increased risk for development of psychosis, increased risk for cognitive impairment,” Robinson Barrett said.

She also highlighted people who are genetically vulnerable, or have a family history of mental illness as well as heavy users who smoke regularly.

While cannabis has many cannabinoids, Robinson Barrett explained that the main ones are Delta-9-THC, which most people know as a psychoactive component, and CBD, which can have a calming or relaxing effect.

Kazaara agreed that cannabis misuse can complicate mental health treatment.

“Yes, it does. Cannabis complicates the treatment of psychiatric conditions. For example, in the case of schizophrenia, it can worsen symptoms and also make the medication we use for it, less effective,” he explained.

In the meantime, Atkinson stressed that the NCDA was not demonising cannabis, highlighting the medicinal benefits and scope for a medicinal industry.

“We recognise the value, but we see the downside in our clients and in some of the young people who we have to treat,” she explained.

She urged that use must be balanced with ensuring that the population, especially youth and those with a predisposition to mental illness, understand the risk of use, particularly in a problematic manner.

World.title: Honorary consul to Atlanta Elaine Grant-Bryan ‘humbled’ by OD recognition
World.content:
Elaine Grant-Bryan

When Elaine Grant-Bryan settled in Atlanta in 1990, that city was long acknowledged as the mecca of black empowerment in the United States. She joined a growing Jamaican community which has made an impact in commerce and community politics.

Grant-Bryan has been Jamaica’s honorary consul to Atlanta since 2018. Currently in her third term, she has been awarded the Order of Distinction (Officer class) by the Jamaican government for service to the diaspora.

That award will be presented during the National Honours and Awards ceremony on October 19 at King’s House in Kingston.

In an interview with Observer Online, Grant-Bryan spoke of being “deeply humbled” by recognition of her work. Like New York City and South Florida, she said Jamaicans have made their mark in Atlanta and neighbouring areas such as Decatur and Stone Mountain.

“This region has grown significantly, especially after COVID-19 as Jamaicans moved from colder regions in the United States in great numbers. Our community has doubled, and many have successfully assimilated in the Georgia culture and made significant contributions to Jamaica and this region,” Grant-Bryan stated.

An educator and real estate broker, she points to initiatives started with her husband Gregory as major achievements of her tenure. These include the Elaine Bryan Foundation which drives the Jamaican Pioneer Programme and STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics).

The pioneer programme allows Americans of Jamaican heritage to gain citizenship in their family’s homeland. Once that is secured, they increase their contribution to Jamaica’s education system by mentoring and assisting needy students.

STEAM is an enrichment curriculum she developed with her husband, a programmer and Information Technology expert. It teaches coding/programming and offers career assessments, internships, entrepreneurships, and scholarships to Jamaican students completing degrees in STEAM fields.

Empowerment was a buzz word in Elaine Bryan’s home in Kingston, where she was born to a father who was an engineer and her mother, a nurse. A past student of Excelsior and Kingston Technical high schools, she was head girl at the latter.

Staying true to her profession, education is the thrust of upcoming projects by the Elaine Bryan Foundation.

“We will continue to include additional students who are completing degrees in the STEAM fields in Jamaica. The projection for 2026-7 is to extend mentorship programmes in Jamaica, study abroad and exchange programmes,” she disclosed.

World.title: ‘Long overdue’
World.content:
Minister of National Security and Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang and Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange are all smiles as they receive the keys to the third Government-run shelter for women facing domestic abuse. (Photo: JIS)

LOCAL gender advocates have welcomed news that work has been completed on a third shelter for victims of domestic abuse.

Minister with responsibility for gender affairs Olivia Grange made the announcement last Friday as she toured the facility at an undisclosed location.

“We made a commitment that we would establish three centres, safe spaces for women, and we have achieved that,” said Grange as she pointed out that prior to the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration there were no State-run shelters for women wishing to leave violent relationships.

In the last few years the Government completed, and is operating, two shelters for women. Grange said the addition of the third shelter will enable the ministry to offer up to 70 safe spaces for women and their children.

Grange said the completion of this third shelter, which is scheduled to begin providing a safe space for women after September 1, enables the Government to provide much-needed services to vulnerable females across the entire island.

“The completion of this space advances the gender agenda, because what we have been able to do now is to provide the spaces across the island, and we are now better equipped that when we get the call we are able to activate the kind of network that is necessary to move [women in abusive situations] into safe spaces,” said Grange.

On Sunday, gender and development practitioner Judith Wedderburn told the Jamaica Observer that the new shelter was long overdue.

“It is certainly very welcome because, not only from my experience but from the reports of women who do suffer, they have been beaten by a male partner and have experienced gender-based violence. The data does show us that it’s not getting better. More and more reports are coming out that it is happening,” said Wedderburn

According to Wedderburn, she became aware of plans to construct the new shelter through discussions with officials of the Bureau of Gender Affairs, however she was uncertain of the completion time.

“I am acknowledging that I have been in meetings in the last couple months where it was reported by somebody from the bureau that a third shelter was going to be built in a different part of the island, outside of Kingston. My understanding was it was going to serve the western part of the island,” said Wedderburn.

Pointing to a recent article published by the Jamaica Gleaner headlined, ‘The cop who finally listened’, Wedderburn said the presence of another shelter in the country serves as a call to action.

“Two women who recounted years of fear after ending abusive relationships are grateful to a corporal for standing with them. What it said was the woman who had been so badly abused was paying tribute to the only policeman who took her report seriously, the only policeman that supported her. And if you reflect on not just this article but other reports, on many occasions, unfortunately, a woman will not gather up the strength to go to a police station to report the incident,” Wedderburn argued.

Welcoming the initiative Joy Crawford, co-founder and executive director of female support group Eve for Life, told the Observer that the move strengthens the national response to gender-based violence (GBV) and expands access to safety for women and children leaving abusive situations.

“We recommend convening a robust, national GBV shelter working group comprising Government, NGOs, community-based organisations and other stakeholders to improve coordination, effectiveness, and accountability across the shelter system. This should include deliberate efforts to strengthen and expand non-government shelter models, recognising that Government cannot do this alone,” said Crawford.

She told the Observer that the country needs more diverse, accessible safe spaces across the island for survivors with different needs, including women with children, women with complex needs, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.

“NGOs and community organisations play vital roles in victim identification, referral, psychosocial support, and sustained engagement. Formal referral pathways and partnerships can help survivors access appropriate services and safe accommodation earlier,” added Crawford.

For advocacy officer at Jamaica Coalition for a Healthy Society Philippa Davies, the provision of a third shelter by the Government is a commendable initiative but it is unfortunate that the problem of GBV exists.

“It is always better that society encourages, teaches, and supports healthy, safe relationships between men and women. As such, the family is the fundamental foundational institution of any society. The very real need for such places is evidence of family pathology, which is often passed on through generations,” said Davies.

She argued that the Government needs to establish a Ministry of the Family to address the critical role of the family and the need to prioritise its welfare.

“This would include strongly encouraging women and men to exercise discernment when choosing romantic and life partners, and to seek wise advice before and when challenges arise. It is scientifically established that the brain hormones released during sex bonds partners to the point of overshadowing danger signals such as the potential for or the occurrence of abuse,” added Davies who argued that the Government should also consider providing support for men who may be victims of abuse.

In announcing the completion of the new facility Grange said the Government-run shelters not only provide safety but also provide a therapeutic environment for women to rebuild their lives.

“We not only ensure that we protect them, but we help them to gain skills where they don’t have skills, we provide counselling, we have adequate space that we can facilitate a family — mother and children,” said Grange.

She revealed that during the last few years, one shelter hosted a mother and five of her children, while another mother gave birth while residing at another shelter.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang, acting in his capacity as chairman of the Citizens Business Group — a Government team that is mandated to manage social interventions across the country — said the establishment of Government-run shelters for women has been a big part of a programme to seek to impact, in a positive way, a number of vulnerable communities in Jamaica and, in particular in this case, women who have suffered abuse.

Chang noted that in the past few years the ministry has established domestic violence intervention centres at selected police stations as part of the strategy to eliminate domestic violence.

World.title: UN chief tells countries to rein in autonomous weapons
World.content:
Guterres and ICRC chief Mirjana Spoljaric underlined that targeting civilians in war is a violation of international humanitarian law, and said they fear that machines won't be able to tell the difference between combatants and non-combatants.

Both called for a ban on autonomous weapons which produce unpredictable results and anti-personnel weapons that deliberately target human beings.

The UN is set to hold a conference in Geneva in November to review its treaty on conventional weapons. Lethal autonomous weapon systems are expected to be a subject of that gathering. The UN has long been pushing countries to progress on legally binding rules.

"When we speak about AI, we want human oversight," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the Commission's assessment on whether humans should be kept in the loop of military applications.

Human oversight is a key concept of the bloc's Artificial Intelligence Act, which doesn't apply, though, to defence or security applications.

World.title: Wie verändert Künstliche Intelligenz den Krieg? — mit Sven Weizenegger
World.content:

Der vereitelte Drohnenanschlag am Flughafen Leipzig/Halle hat gezeigt, wie verwundbar kritische Infrastruktur in Deutschland sein kann. Eine mutmaßlich sprengstoffbeladene Drohne, nur wenige Meter von einem ukrainischen Antonow-Frachtflugzeug entfernt. Gleichzeitig verändert sich Kriegsführung in der Ukraine und im Nahen Osten rasant: Drohnen erkennen Ziele selbstständig, Algorithmen unterstützen militärische Entscheidungen, Künstliche Intelligenz ist längst Teil des Schlachtfelds.

Wo steht Deutschland dabei? Ist die Bundeswehr auf diese Entwicklung vorbereitet? Darüber spricht Rixa Fürsen mit Sven Weizenegger, der den Cyber Innovation Hub der Bundeswehr leitet – die digitale Innovationseinheit der Streitkräfte. Seine Aufgabe: neue Technologien schneller in die Truppe bringen und die Bundeswehr auf den Krieg von morgen vorbereiten. Das Besondere: Weizenegger ist kein Soldat, sondern Hacker.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

World.title: Waymo will 2027 in München  autonome Robotaxis fahren lassen
World.content:
Google-Tochter startet damit erstmals in Deutschland und der EU. Bayern sieht sich als Vorreiter beim autonomen Fahren.

MÜNCHEN – Waymo will bis Ende 2027 selbstfahrenden Robotaxis in München an den Start bringen. Das gab das US-Unternehmen am Dienstag bekannt.

Die Google-Tochter beginnt noch in diesem Jahr damit, seine Fahrzeuge in München einzusetzen. Sie werden zunächst manuell gesteuert, während das Unternehmen „mit der hochauflösenden Kartierung des lokalen Straßennetzes beginnt“ und das autonome System mit Sicherheitsfahrern testet, teilte Waymo mit.

„Bayern ist entschlossen, seiner Vorreiterrolle gerecht zu werden und international eine führende Position im Bereich des autonomen Fahrens einzunehmen“, sagte Florian Herrmann, Leiter der Bayerischen Staatskanzlei. „Jetzt müssen wir zügig vom Testbetrieb zum Einsatz in der Praxis übergehen.“

World.title: Waymo to launch robotaxis in Munich in 2027
World.content:
This article is also available in: German

Waymo will introduce its self-driving taxis in Munich by the end of 2027, the American autonomous driving company announced today.

The Google subsidiary will start rolling out vehicles in the German city this year, which will be manually driven while the company "starts with high-definition mapping of local street networks" and testing with safety drivers, Waymo said in a statement.

"Bavaria is determined to live up to its pioneering role and be an international leader in autonomous driving," Florian Herrmann, the head of the Bavarian state chancellery, said in the statement. "Now we need to move quickly from testing to real-world deployment.”

World.title: State-backed hackers targeted EU officials on WhatsApp, document shows
World.content:
The officials were the targets of so-called “state-sponsored spearphishing,” the presentation said, a term for state-backed, targeted and bespoke campaigns to get specific people to click on dodgy links or open malicious attachments. Hackers used "social engineering techniques" to trick EU officials, crafting personalized messages that were more likely to get targets to take the bait.

Earlier this year, POLITICO first reported that the European Commission told some of its most senior officials to shut down a Signal group over hacking fears. It came at the same time as a series of warnings by national cyber authorities telling governments to move away from commercial messaging apps like WhatsApp and Signal for official business.

In March, at least five national cyber and intelligence agencies publicly warned about ongoing hacking campaigns on Signal and WhatsApp. Dutch intelligence services specifically pinned this on Russia, and Germany warned that hackers were targeting “high-ranking individuals in politics, the military, and diplomacy, as well as investigative journalists.”

The agencies warned then that hackers were posing as a fake Signal support chatbot to persuade users to share their codes, allowing them to take over an account to read incoming communications and group chats.

EU cybersecurity officials said in the presentation that the bloc's institutions had faced eight "significant incidents" so far this year. One key challenge, they flagged, is that the different EU institutions still use different technical cybersecurity solutions and lack a common solution to exchange sensitive and classified documents.

The European Commission declined to give details on internal security practices in response to POLITICO's questions on the presentation.

WhatsApp and Signal did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

World.title: Putin allows government takeover of firms vulnerable to drone attacks
World.content:
Smoke rises from a warehouse near St. Petersburg in Russia after being hit by Ukrainian drones on July 24, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

“We are not talking about nationalization,” insisted a top Kremlin official.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has given his government powers to temporarily manage critical infrastructure facilities if their owners fail to protect them against security threats.

A decree published Monday gives Russia’s Federal Agency for State Property Management extensive powers to seize industrial sites if their owners have failed to take protective measures against uncrewed aerial vehicles, among other risks.

It will operate seized businesses as the owner and Putin can designate any other entity as the temporary manager, according to the decree.

World.title: Gun violence rattles Brussels as mayor points to ‘bullet holes in the ground’
World.content:
“A guy fired a Kalashnikov in front of children in my village,” Spinette told reporters. “There are bullet holes in the ground.” Customers at a pizzeria were forced to lie on the floor as shots rang out, Belga reported. The attacker fled the scene and had not been apprehended as of Tuesday morning.

Saint-Gilles has been grappling with drug-related violence for years, particularly around the train station. In June 2024, two people were killed and three others injured when gunmen opened fire with Kalashnikovs at a café near Brussels-Midi station, in an incident authorities linked to drug trafficking. Authorities subsequently stepped up police presence in several hotspots in the area, but not sufficiently, according to Spinette.

“I’ve been asking for reinforcements for three years,” he said.

Around 700 police officers work across Saint-Gilles and the wider Midi police zone, while the municipality increased its annual contribution to the police force by €1.8 million last year. At least 66 shootings have been documented across the wider Brussels region in 2026, Le Soir reports.

“Drug criminals are issuing threats because we are disrupting their operations,” Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told Belgian public broadcaster VRT. “We must continue this fight with determination. It will be a long one.” Quintin said he had already sent 77 additional officers to Brussels and was considering sending more.

World.title: Germany ‘under threat,’ Merz says after another explosive drone found near airport
World.content:
Explosive drones found near Leipzig airport show Germany is "under threat," Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Tuesday after the reported discovery of another device.

"The drone attack in Leipzig, among other things, shows that we are also facing very real threats. Germany has come under increased scrutiny from hybrid attackers," Merz said in remarks ahead of a cabinet retreat in Neuhardenberg.

German counterterrorism authorities opened an investigation on Aug. 5 after an airport worker found a drone carrying an explosive device on which the detonator apparently failed. Investigators found another drone on Aug. 14 near the Leipzig airport, an important logistics base for NATO, the Süddeutsche Zeitung outlet reported Tuesday.

World.title: Houthi strikes threaten to pull Yemen back into full-scale war
World.content:
The Iran-backed Houthis are using regional warfare to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia, while their attacks risk reopening Yemen's own conflict and disrupting shipping in the Red Sea.

Yemen is increasingly at risk of backsliding into full-scale conflict. On Monday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia attacked another crude oil tanker in the Red Sea off the coast of Saudi Arabia. The attack followed earlier strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure and other ships in the nearby Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The waterway connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and has served as an alternative route for oil exports from Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries affected by Iran's ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In August, the Houthis also attacked areas under the control of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, particularly the port city of Mokha. Yemen's internationally recognized government targeted Houthi infrastructure in response.

"Mokha overlooks the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is strategically important to the Houthis," Hisham Al-Omeisy, a Yemeni conflict analyst, told DW. "In the long term, the Houthis want to weaken the government's control over the Red Sea coastal areas and they aim for full control of the governate Al-Hudeydah [of which Mokha is a part] to continue their strategy of exerting pressure on global maritime trade," he predicted.

The current military flare-up ended four years of relative calm between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government, backed by Saudi Arabia.

However, Al-Omeisy notes that there are also two other aspects that drive the latest Houthi strategy.

Following the ceasefire in 2022, Saudi Arabia has continued to support the Yemeni government financially and militarily. Saudi Arabia also never fully lifted its air and port blockades in areas under Houthi control. Despite this, the Houthis consolidated their position as Yemen's de facto rulers. In Al-Omeisy's view, the Houthis now hope to extract additional concessions from Saudi Arabia.

"The Houthis are under a lot of pressure locally to deliver on their promises, for example, to reform the government, pay salaries and improve livelihoods," Al-Omeisy said. He therefore believes that the Houthis are using the wider Middle East war to distract from their failure to deliver in these areas by "saying that we are now busy with another war."

The Houthi strikes are also carefully timed, Al-Omeisy added. "They've learned their lessons from how Iran managed to basically dominate the Strait of Hormuz," he said, adding that the blockade of imports and oil exports leaves Saudi Arabia in a very vulnerable position.

The Houthi militia attacked the port of Mokha which is under the control of the Saudi-backed government in Yemen Image: Khaled Ziad/AFP

Saudi Arabia's balancing act with the Houthi militia

"Instability in Yemen is no longer simply a problem on Saudi Arabia's southern border," Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based consulting firm Azure Strategy, told DW.

"Ultimately, Saudi Arabia wants a more secure Red Sea, but also wants to achieve that without becoming trapped in another war in Yemen," she added.

"Saudi Arabia's priority is protecting the economic transformation under Vision 2030 which also explains why Saudi Arabia increasingly sees the Red Sea as one connected theater rather than separate crises in Yemen, Sudan and the Horn of Africa," Gower said, noting that Houthi attacks threaten shipping, raise insurance costs, deter investors and disrupt the infrastructure on which Vision 2030 increasingly depends.

In turn, Saudi Arabia has updated its defense policy, she also noted in a recent op-ed. "Riyadh has been focusing on building a broader security architecture that could reduce the burden of defending its maritime interests."

Earlier in July, Saudi Arabia spearheaded the creation of a multinational Maritime Defense Alliance with more than 14 countries, including Saudi Arabia's strong ally and Iran's adversary, the United States.

"The new Saudi-led maritime coalition is part of that approach as it allows Riyadh to spread the security burden, strengthen regional deterrence and counter threats across the Bab el-Mandeb, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden as part of the same security problem," Gower said, adding that it is yet to be proven to be effective.

In August, Saudi Arabia also joined a defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. However, analysts again point out that this new pact is yet to show "operational relevance."



For Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, none of these coalitions and alliances will actually help Saudi Arabia avoid being dragged back into war in Yemen. In an interview with the Financial Times newspaper he said that "they either give the Houthis $5 billion and allow them to fly directly to Tehran, allow them to dock any ship at their ports, and hope they are not going to come back in a few years and ask for $10 billion…or you use that $5 billion to support your anti-Houthi coalition of Yemenis to push the Houthis to get down from their high horse and negotiate."

Analysts say that the Houthis learned from Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz before they started their own blockade of Saudi ships in the Red Sea Image: Media Office of the Ministry of Transport - Republic of Yemen/Handout/REUTERS

Humanitarian situation depends on a peaceful roadmap

For the population, neither of these scenarios spell hope for real peace. According to the United Nations, Yemen is still suffering from one of the world's worst humanitarian crises after years of war between 2014 and 2022. More than half the population is in need of humanitarian assistance. "I urge all parties to halt immediately any actions that risk returning Yemen to full-scale conflict," the UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk warned in a recent statement .

"It feels impossible to imagine worse conditions for people in Yemen right now," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "And yet, renewed conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition threatens to worsen conditions further," she warned.

With Yemen's humanitarian crisis already so severe, the question is whether the latest escalation in Yemen can still be contained through diplomacy.

For the Yemeni Nobel Peace Prize laureate and human rights defender Tawakkol Karman, any serious peace effort must begin by addressing the root cause of the crisis: the collapse of the Yemeni state and the undermining of its institutions.

In a recent meeting with representatives of UN Security Council member states, Karman said that in her view, the National Dialogue outcomes — reached through consensus among all Yemeni components including the Houthis, under UN auspices and with the endorsement of the Security Council — remain the most realistic roadmap for peace.

World.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on US goods
World.content:
Canada's government said it would impose tariffs on some 700 US goods as of next month, amid the latest trade spat between Donald Trump and Mark Carney.

Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States , as relations between the neighbors faltered following failed trade talks last week.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa also announced financial support for businesses and workers impacted by the latest dispute with the Trump administration.

It listed some 700 US products that would be subject to either 15%, 25% or 50% tariffs as of September 8, in steps designed to match those announced earlier in the week by US President Donald Trump.

The US is Canada's largest trading partner, and Canada is the second largest for the US, trailing only fellow neighbor Mexico. Several such disputes have marked both of Trump's terms.

What did Canada say about the measures?

Canada's Finance Ministry said in a statement that the government had negotiated "intensively and in good faith" with the US towards a "fair and comprehensive trade agreement."

"In recent days, however, the US proposed new terms that were not in Canada’s best interest, basically, asking too much of Canada, and offering too little in return," the Ministry wrote, saying that at this point it suspended talks rather than accepting a "bad deal."

"Canada did not choose this trade conflict, but we need to respond to provide a level playing field to our businesses," it said.

Finance Minsiter Francois-Philippe Champagne described the measures as "dollar-for-dollar, rate for rate counter-tariffs," as well as a "multi-billion dollar support package will protect workers, farmers, families, and businesses."

"Canada's counter tariffs will apply to products covering $27.6 billion in imports from the U.S. and will focus on sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, that are most impacted by U.S. tariffs," the ministry said, naming the same figure as the US in its announcement.

Here's what you need to know about the backdrop to this flare-up:

Washington ‌and ​Ottawa were racing to reach an agreement beforeUS President Donald Trump's steep new US tariffs, announced in July, were due to take effect

Talks broke down days after the US President announced the neighbors were close to agreeing to a trade deal

The collapse in negotiations triggered Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods the next day

Why is Canada imposing new tariffs?

While the US and Canada have shared one of the world’s largest trade relationships, the recent talks signal a breakdown in relations.

"An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States" is "not something we’re going to accept," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

"We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum," Carney said, opting for an even blunter approach in French. "That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal."

US-Canada trade war: The cost of fighting back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What had the US said?

Donald Trump returned to the topic of Canada early on Tuesday on social media, claiming the US was mulling renaming Lake Ontario, the only one of the five North American Great Lakes named after a Canadian territory.

"The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to doing [sic] much business with them any longer," Trump wrote.

His administration "renamed" the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America soon after Trump returned to the White House last year — a change that almost nobody besides the US government has implemented. Even US tech giant Google shows it as the Gulf of Mexico first on its maps for users everywhere but in the US.

A day earlier, Trump had threatened he would impose a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel from January 1, 2027, and took to social media to unleash a tirade against the historic partner.

Trump hits Canada with 50% tariffs in major trade escalation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"On trade, ‌and in other ways, also, ‌they ​are among the worst nations in the world to deal with. They feel entitled, and ​yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" the US president said.

Canada relies heavily on the US as its top trading partner, with American-bound exports making up 70% of the country's total. The relationship runs both ways, too: government data shows Canada was the second-largest US trading partner in goods this year, just behind Mexico.

No further negotiations are currently scheduled.

World.title: Schalke coach looks to Bosnia bond in Bundesliga return
World.content:
After three seasons in the second division, Schalke are back in the Bundesliga. Just a year ago, few would have guessed that their revival would largely be 'Made in Bosnia.'

"A year ago, I told my team that we need to step things up by two gears, and we did that," Schalke's second-year coach, Miron Muslic, told the club's website ahead of this season's return to the Bundesliga.

"Now we need to step things up by two gears all over again. At first glance it may sound like a threat, too dramatic, but this is what we will need to meet this challenge. The lads know this and we are confident that we have a higher gear in us."

The challenge for Muslic is not simply to avoid relegation in year one after three seasons in the second division, but to "establish ourselves in the Bundesliga."

It will also be Muslic's first season in the Bundesliga after he succeeded where several of his predecessors failed – guiding the Royal Blues back to the topflight.

'Where did this guy come from?'

It's something few would have predicted just over a year ago, when he was unveiled as Schalke's new head coach. Many, if not most, of the club's supporters will have been left scrolling on their phones to try to figure out just who he was. It's a point not lost on the Austrian coach, who fled the Bosnian War with his parents at the age of nine.

"Many were wondering; 'Who is this guy, where did he come from?'" Muslic, who joined from lower league English club Plymouth Argyle, told German football magazine "kicker" last October, after Schalke had climbed to the top of the standings for the first time in the campaign.

That's where they finished the first half of the season. But during the January transfer window, Muslic and sporting director Frank Baumann still weren't sure the squad had what it would take to guarantee a top-two finish – and automatic promotion – at the end of the campaign.

Proven goal scorer looking for playing time

Then the final piece to the promotion puzzle fell into Muslic's lap. Bosnia captain Edin Dzeko, a striker who has been prolific virtually everywhere he has played, was largely languishing on the bench at Italian club Fiorentina, and looking for playing time. He let it be known that he was prepared to take a major pay cut to help Schalke achieve promotion. By the time they'd done just that, he had contributed six goals to the cause – and just turned 40.

Many expected Dzeko to hang up his boots after he captained Bosnia in just their second appearance at the World Cup this past summer. However, a couple of weeks before the start of the season, Dzeko confirmed that he would make his return to the Bundesliga – 15 seasons after he last played in the league with Wolfsburg. After signing a one-year, bonus-heavy contract, Dzeko said that while he had "three other options" he made up his mind that if he was to continue playing, it would only be at Schalke.

Edin Dzeko captained Bosnia at this summer's World Cup in North America Image: Mutsu Kawamori/AFLOSPORT/IMAGO

Dzeko 'still hungry' at 40

"Winning promotion to the Bundesliga is one of the highlights of my career," Dzeko told the club's website.

"I'm still hungry. And I want to help our team in the Bundesliga, too."

Just how much action Dzeko will see in the Bundesliga is unclear. However, Muslic, who is understood to have pushed hard to bring his countryman back for another year, believes he can still be a difference maker in key situations.

Still, he isn't expected to see as much playing time as the third member of Schalke's Bosnian triumvirate, central defender Nikola Katic, whose winding road to Gelsenkirchen saw him work with Muslic a few years ago at Plymouth. Even before Dzeko arrived in Gelsenkirchen last winter, he and Katic already knew each other from the national team.

'Once Schalke, always Schalke,' but...

Now all three are committed to ensuring that Schalke's return to the Bundesliga is more than a one-season excursion, and Muslic, whose contract runs through the end of the 2027-28 season, hopes he will remain in charge for years to come.

"I will remain a member of Schalke 04 forever — 100 percent. No matter how our paths might part one day," the coach told "kicker" last October.



Nikola Katic has established himself as a stallwart in Schalke's central defense Image: Alex Gottschalk/DeFodi Images/IMAGO

At the same time, he's realistic enough to know that as a coach, he won't be in Gelsenkirchen forever. While his current focus is all about Schalke, he already knows where he would like to wind up somewhere down the road.

"I would like to be the national team coach of Bosnia-Herzegovina one day," he said.

"And I believe it will happen. The fundamental prerequisites are simply a perfect fit — my background, my connection, and the love for my home country."

For now though, the focus is on the new season; Schalke were left licking their wounds after fourth-tier Halle took them to extra time in their first-round German Cup match on Monday – before emerging with a 5-2 win. Dzeko, who had come on in the 64th minute expecting to play only half an hour, scored two of Schalke's goals.

Ever the optimist, Muslic said afterwards that the hard-fought result not only proved that "we'll need Edin" in the Bundesliga season, but that Schalke had also demonstrated their "resilience."

Next comes the first real test of whether Schalke can indeed kick it up a couple of gears, when they make their Bundsliga return in Augsburg on Sunday.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

World.title: How Germany's drone defense fails
World.content:
Drone defense is a priority for the German government. Several dramatic incidents involving explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport show there are still substantial shortcomings.

On August 25, German media reported on a third drone allegedly found near Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. A drone and a substance — which initial assessments suggest could be around 50 grams of Hexogen, a highly explosive military-grade explosive — were reportedly discovered in a field outside the airport grounds. Consequently, public broadcasters NDR and WDR, and the daily broadsheet Süddeutsche Zeitung are speculating about a plot that may be far more extensive than what has been publicly disclosed so far.

Speaking on the sidelines of a federal government retreat in the state of Brandenburg, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) stated: "Germany has increasingly come into the crosshairs of hybrid attackers."

Merz also pointed to measures aimed at better protecting the public. Just a few days ago, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) inaugurated a drone security research center in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, not far from Leipzig and Halle in Saxony.

How could drones laden with explosives fly unhindered near or into Leipzig/Halle airport and remain unnoticed for at least several hours? Interior Minister Dobrindt had immediately spoken of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."

Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because one drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.

However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.

Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, security expert Nico Lange warned.

"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.

Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense.

"That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.

The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.

Coordinated response difficult for state, federal police

Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.

In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.

Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.

Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Unclear responsibilities

Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities.

"The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.

Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.

Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.

Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?

As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.

A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.

In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."

German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Airports, train stations still lack protection

There is also a lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.

"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."

The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.

The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on August 14, 2026, and updated on August 25 to reflect news developments.

World.title: Will Volkswagen's crunch week decide Germany's auto future?
World.content:
Volkswagen bosses face angry workers this week over restructuring plans that could eliminate up to 100,000 jobs and threaten several German plants. DW examines the pressure on Europe's biggest automaker.

1. Why is Volkswagen holding crunch talks with workers?

Volkswagen's management is holding extraordinary meetings with workers this week amid an unprecedented cost-cutting drive, including reports of up to 100,000 job losses and the possible closure of several German car factories.

Germany's auto industry faces a deep structural crisis due to intense pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), higher production costs and other challenges.

As Europe's biggest carmaker by volume, VW has the heaviest exposure to overcapacity in its German plants, high fixed costs and its reliance on China.

Workers have been particularly concerned by how the restructuring was communicated so far, which representatives have described as "disastrous."

Nine separate meetings will be held, starting on Tuesday at VW's headquarters in Wolfsburg, with talks at other sites including Emden, Zwickau, Braunschweig and Hanover before the end of the week.

Workers had already agreed to around 50,000 job cuts, mainly through voluntary redundancy schemes. But management now thinks a further 50,000 jobs will have to be lost.

Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume has warned the carmaker's troubles could get worse Image: Malte Ossowski/Sven Simon/picture alliance

2. Why does Volkswagen need to make such drastic cuts?

CEO Oliver Blume has stressed that VW is in a "more than critical state" and that the measures adopted so far are not enough to restore competitiveness.

"We are oversized. That often makes us too slow and too complicated," he told staff in an interview on the company's intranet last week.

With nearly 630,000 workers, VW has grown more bloated than its peers over decades after choosing to control more stages of production — including components and software — while mopping up rivals such as Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti.

The automaker was also slow to transition to EVs just as Chinese competitors gained ground, causing a large sales drop in its former number one market — China.

Blume warned that VW is currently over-producing around half a million vehicles in Europe every year.

While closing German factories would be a last resort, Blume said management "cannot currently see any way of them remaining profitable in the 2030s."

Other automakers have criticized Germany's high operating costs, including Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius, who last month spoke of a 70% cost gap between the firm's Hungarian and German operations.

3. What reaction is expected from workers?

Blume is expected to face an angry reaction from VW employees, who rank as some of the best-paid auto workers in the world thanks to the power and influence of unions and the works council.

After already accepting VW's earlier restructuring plans, Christiane Benner, the head of the IG Metall union, said workers "are getting another slap in the face."

During the meeting with workers in Wolfsburg on Tuesday, VW works council chair ‌Daniela Cavallo said "trust" in Blume and the executive board "has been ‌damaged," but "not yet beyond repair."

Last month, VW's supervisory board — which includes shareholders and worker representatives — rejected the second round of cost-cutting proposals.

The move is further complicated as VW is part-owned by the state of Lower Saxony, which holds 20% of the voting rights. The state has refused to sign off on the plans, according to German media reports.

"Lower Saxony is automotive country ... and this must remain so," said Olaf Lies, the state's premier on Monday. "Now it is important to me that we find joint ​solutions."

Volkswagen workers in Germany could face big layoffs due to red tape, US tariffs and rising competition from China, says management Image: Moritz Frankenberg/picture alliance/dpa

4. How is Volkswagen planning on getting back on track?

Blume told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper last weekend that he had drawn up "the largest transformation plan in the history of the Volkswagen Group."

His Target Vision 2030 plan aims to cut VW's model lineup by half and lower overheads, particularly in Germany. The automaker will also reduce its global production target, which peaked at about 11 million vehicles in 2018, to 9 million a year in the future.

Faced with rising competition from China, along with US tariffs, geopolitics and red tape, Blume warned that VW management has to "assume the risks will get worse, worldwide."

Most global automakers are struggling to react to Chinese EVs flooding global markets, increasingly unpredictable markets and the mounting pressure of EU net-zero rules, which include fines for not hitting emissions targets.

Blume told the newspaper that the next few years would be "decisive" in determining which carmakers remain viable.

He said although VW achieved a solid 3.8% operating margin, the profits are not enough to invest in new technologies, products and maintain the company's sites.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: Germans swap friends for screens in their free time
World.content:
People are spending less time going out with friends and more of their leisure time online. AI is now part of that shift.

Germans are spending less of their free time socializing with friends and more on individually planned and digital activities, according to a survey published on Tuesday .

Meeting friends remains the most important social leisure activity, but its role has weakened significantly over time.

How Germans are spending their free time now

The Hamburg Foundation for Future Studies found that just 19% of 3,000 respondents said they regularly went out with friends, down from 37% when its first "Leisure Monitor" was conducted 40 years ago.

"Traditional sociability is losing reach, while social contacts are increasingly shifting toward individually planned and digital forms," said Ulrich Reinhardt, the foundation's scientific director.

He said everyday leisure was increasingly dominated by internet use, television, music and smartphones. Digital activities have grown sharply:

82% listen to music digitally at least weekly, up from 52% in 2016.

71% use social media weekly, up from 48%.

33% play video games weekly, up from 9%.

Artificial intelligence is now used at least once a week by 42% of respondents, rising to 62% among 18- to 24-year-olds.

How deep can a relationship with AI get? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reinhardt said younger users were turning to AI not just for information, but also for advice, reassurance and, in some cases, as a substitute for friendship.

Are Germans becoming less active?

Surprisingly, the survey found that Germans were more physically active than they once were.

The survey found that 53% now exercise at least once a week, compared with just 18% in 1986.

Doing nothing or simply relaxing has also become more common, rising 15 percentage points since 2016 to 62%.

The popularity of joining clubs has remained stable, with 18% taking part weekly in sports, singing or other associations. Regular volunteering has even increased, from 6% 40 years ago to 12% today.

World.title: Nigeria's jet fuel conundrum: Scarcity at home, abundance abroad
World.content:
Nigeria is fast becoming Europe's biggest jet fuel supplier, as it continues to help ease ongoing shortages abroad. Meanwhile at home, the West African country’s own airlines are struggling to keep their tanks full.

For the past two months. Nigeria has emerged as Europe's largest supplier of jet fuel, overtaking the United States.

The 650,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) mega refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, outside Lagos has evolved into an increasingly important source of fuel for the continent following supply disruptions caused by the Iran war.

During last year's peak summer months, the majority of these supplies still originated from the Middle East.

But since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, Europe has been relying on imports of roughly 700,000 bpd in total to meet the present demands of the aviation industry, according to the private, global trade intelligence business Kpler.

Dry fuel tanks in Europe

In fact, back in April, the head of the International Energy Agency Fatih Birol expressed concern that at the time Europe only had "maybe six weeks or so" of jet fuel supplies remaining.

Less than two months later, four airports in northern Italy — Bologna, Venice, Treviso and Milan's Linate — even introduced temporary restrictions on jet fuel use, imposing a ceiling of 2,000 liters per aircraft for short-haul journeys, according to local media, while giving priority to medical and long-haul flights.

Europe has, in the meantime, been able to absorb the shock of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by diversifying its resources and boosting supplies from countries like Nigeria — but at what cost?

Africa's fuel crisis: Is Dangote the answer? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Paradox of surplus production

Nigeria continues to produce a record amount of jet fuel through the Dangote refinery, equivalent to about 24 million liters each day, with much of this now being shipped to Europe.

But domestic airlines in the West African country meanwhile appear to struggle to keep up with their daily estimated needs because of the surge in prices and the demands of the free market.

Ikemesit Effiong, a partner at the Africa-focused SBM intelligence consultancy, explained that "Nigeria operates a fully deregulated downstream market where Dangote prices its products with reference to international parity, not preferential domestic rates."

"Fuel flows to wherever pays the most," he told DW, adding that "currently, that is Europe, not Lagos."

"The key lesson Nigerian players are learning is that production capacity alone does not guarantee affordability at home."

While the Dangote refinery has significantly improved fuel availability in the country, which has long been plagued by chronic fuel scarcity and long queues at petrol stations, domestic prices are still among the highest on the continent.

Passengers in Nigeria are likely to think twice before purchasing flights, as prices have skyrocketed Image: Benson Ibeabuchi/AFP/Getty Images

Local airlines struggle to keep up

In the fully deregulated Nigerian market, regional airlines also have to compete with international buyers, who typically place orders for greater purchasing volumes, often without any middlemen involved between them at the refineries; according to Effiong, this alone leave global players with significant negotiating advantages compared to smaller local companies.

"The result is that [while] domestic airlines might be physically closer to the refinery, they're economically less competitive in accessing its products. They might as well be halfway across the world," he added.

Since the beginning of the crisis, local aviation operators have reportedly accrued over 60bn Naira ($45 million; €38 million) in debt to local banks to be able to sustain operations and keep afloat during this surge in prices.

Many operators have even been forced to cut key routes and hike up ticket prices, resulting in frustration and discontent among passengers; furthermore, ongoing flight cancellations and delays only keep adding to the overall sense of dissatisfaction among travelers.

At one point, jet fuel prices jumped up over threefold soon after the start of the Iran war; they have since fallen to a minimum about 1,600 Naira per liter — which compares to roughly 900 Naira prior to the war.

Hidden costs and mark-ups

The current situation is further exacerbated by the abolition of government subsidies for oil products, as well as by Nigeria's state oil company's crude-backed loans.

This means that part of the country's future crude production to is allocated to repaying debts, leaving the Dangote Refinery to have to import its crude to refine — rather than making use of Nigeria's own reserves.

Why Nigeria's largest refinery is importing US oil To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the problem isn't solely focused on the source of the jet fuel itself. Charles Victor, an energy analyst based in Lagos, explained that "[t]he journey from the refinery gate to the airport is expensive with extra layers of additional cost. [These issues include] storage, coastal shipping, moving fuel between tanks, with several traders in between — and each one takes a cut."

Victor went as far as saying that "the problem was never a supply issue. It's what happens to the price on the way to the aircraft."

No solutions without government intervention?

For Victor, the solution is to reserve a certain metric ton amount of fuel for Nigerian airlines each month, and selling this directly and equitably to all stakeholders as a group.

Buying "directly from the refinery gate, if possible, will cut out most of the middlemen adding cost along the way," he told DW, saying that wholesale price could thus at least stabilize around 1,200 Naira pet liter this way.

This plan would also require improved airport storage and distribution infrastructures to "reduce logistics costs that add significantly to the final prices," Ikemesit added. "Finally, the government should institute policies that encourage sustainable commercial relationships between Dangote and domestic carriers."

But would Dangote play along with that? The Dangote Refinery, operating at its maximum capacity of 650,000 bpd, was originally built with the intention of transforming the continent's biggest oil producer into a net exporter of refined products, and thus to end its dependence on fuel imports.

However, with a global crisis situation firmly putting Dangote on the map as a worldwide supplier, that plan might remain a pipe dream.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?
World.content:
Iranian lawmakers have again raised the possibility of leaving a decades-old international nuclear weapons treaty. Analysts say the threat to quit may offer Tehran more leverage than an actual withdrawal.

Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran's nuclear program and its standoff with the United States continue.

Iranian MP Ghasem Ravanbakhsh said a proposal to withdraw from the landmark treaty had been submitted and was being considered.

Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said a withdrawal would be the "best response" to increased US economic pressure.

The idea is not new. Iranian officials and lawmakers have repeatedly raised it during periods of tension with Western governments. However, it remains unclear whether Tehran is actually preparing to leave the treaty or whether the threat itself is the objective.

What would leaving the nuclear treaty mean?

In 1970, Iran ratified the agreement, which is the main international treaty on nuclear non-proliferation.

Iran has been repeatedly accused of having hidden its nuclear program Image: Planet Labs PBC/AP/picture alliance

The NPT has 191 member states and is based on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursuing nuclear disarmament.

Any member can withdraw if it believes that extraordinary events related to the treaty have put its supreme national interests at risk.

It must give three months' notice to the other members and the UN Security Council and explain its reasons. Leaving the treaty is therefore legally possible.

Behrooz Bayat, a nuclear expert and former consultant to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), told DW that the process would take time.

"A withdrawal would almost certainly be seen internationally as a signal that Iran intends either to keep open the option of developing nuclear weapons or to move toward doing so," Bayat said.

He said such a perception could sharply increase political and economic pressure and potentially raise the risk of further military action.

For that reason, Bayat believes Tehran's repeated threats are more useful as diplomatic leverage than as a policy it actually intends to pursue.

Why withdrawal may not benefit Tehran

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst and researcher at LUISS University in Rome, told DW that the renewed debate should be seen in the context of stalled negotiations over uranium enrichment and Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran has about 440 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%, according to the IAEA.

Inspectors from the UN's nuclear watchdog were unable to verify the location of much of the material after the June 2025 US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities.

Iran has already sharply reduced international oversight. In July 2025, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian signed legislation to suspend access for IAEA inspectors into the country until the "security" of its nuclear facilities is guaranteed.

That created what Modarres describes as a potentially more useful position for Tehran than formally withdrawing from the treaty.

"Withdrawal would remove that ambiguity without offering any clear advantage, turning a dispute over compliance into an explicit declaration of intent," the analyst said.

"By remaining formally within the NPT while limiting inspections, Iran can maintain uncertainty about its capabilities and intentions without openly leaving the global non-proliferation system," he added. "Withdrawing would remove much of that uncertainty."

A countdown could increase military risk

Withdrawal could also have security implications for Tehran. Under Article X of the treaty, states must give three months' notice before withdrawing. That period would give Israel, the United States and other governments time to reassess Iran's intentions.

Some analysts argue that governments already concerned about Iran's stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium could interpret a withdrawal as a sign that Tehran was moving closer to a nuclear weapons capability.

US-Iran war: Will it ever end? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bayat said that makes actual withdrawal considerably less attractive than threatening to do so. He added that leaving the treaty could also "complicate Iran's civilian nuclear cooperation."

Membership in the treaty "provides the broader legal and political framework through which non-nuclear states gain access to peaceful nuclear technology," he said. "Russia remains involved in Iran's civilian nuclear sector, particularly at the Bushehr nuclear power plant."

"Formally withdrawing from the treaty could make future cooperation much more difficult politically and legally, even though existing agreements would need to be assessed separately," added Bayat.

Opposition inside Iran

There is no clear consensus in Iran. Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based analyst who has written extensively about Iran's nuclear program, told DW that withdrawing from the treaty has been discussed repeatedly but has never become government policy.

"The issue of leaving the NPT is not new and has been raised many times before," he said. "But right now, there are significant legal and political obstacles, and there is still no full consensus within Iran."

Ghahremanpour said the international community would closely examine any attempt to invoke Article X. He points to the ongoing legal debate over North Korea's withdrawal as an example.

North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003. Although Pyongyang is generally treated internationally as no longer being a party to the treaty, some UN documents note that its formal status remains uncertain.

The treaty itself, however, does not require UN Security Council approval for withdrawal. It requires only that states notify the council.

For Ghahremanpour, the political message is more important than the legal process.

He believes talk of leaving the NPT is mainly aimed at pressuring Washington, and particularly European governments, to make concessions.

Degraded but still dangerous: Iran's evolving threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
