Tech.title: The County Prosecutors Who Became ICE Informants
Tech.content:
This story was produced in partnership with Injustice Watch, a nonprofit newsroom in Chicago focused on the court system.

Rolando Perez Samayoa had come to the US in 2023 seeking safety. Fleeing violence in Mexico, he’d first planned to make a life in Alabama but had been told that Illinois would protect immigrants like him. “There’s some kind of law there,” he said. “It’s supposed to be a sanctuary.”

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

He was referring to the state’s 2017 TRUST Act, which was meant to keep local law enforcement out of federal deportation efforts. Samayoa made his way to southern Illinois and found work cleaning a factory. After a DUI arrest in Marion County last October, Samayoa said, he attended his hearings—a fact confirmed by court records.

In late January, John Christeson, an assistant state’s attorney in the office prosecuting the case, emailed an agent with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, about Samayoa. The message included his date of birth, an upcoming court date, and where he lived: Centralia, Illinois.

“Ok, we’ll take care of it, thank you,” the federal agent, Sergio Fulgencio, wrote back minutes later. Two days later, he wanted to know more: “Do you have any reports on this guy?”

Christeson sent him the police report and related tickets. Three weeks later, federal agents apprehended Samayoa outside his home. They hauled off his 17-year-old son, too.

The exchange is among dozens of emails reviewed by Injustice Watch that reveal a pattern of consequential collaboration between county prosecutors and federal immigration agencies across Illinois during the first 15 months of President Donald Trump’s second term.

State’s attorneys offices in 1 out of every 6 Illinois counties acted as valuable assets of federal immigration enforcement, sharing sensitive personal data about the people they were prosecuting without criminal warrants, public disclosure, or legislative oversight and with no accounting of how often it happened or who was affected.

Tech.title: Optoma GT2400HDR Review: Ace Projector for Golf Simulation
Tech.content:
For less than $1,300, the GT2400HDR is a reasonable option, especially since it works well as a basic golf sim and costs far less than 4K models that can run $5,000 or more. The GT2400HDR also has some interesting perks that make it ideal for long golfing sessions.

For starters, it’s rated for 24/7 continuous operation. That’s because the laser light source doesn’t need to cool down after a few hours and can last 30,000 hours total. (Optoma does recommend powering the unit off when not in use, though.) The laser light source does not use a bulb, so there is nothing to replace. Heat dissipation is amazingly good, as the projector tends to run cool, unlike some high-end models. The GT2400HDR has an IP6X dust rating, so it’s sealed better than some massive home theater projectors that cost $4,000—ironic, considering that if you’re spending that much, you would expect better dust protection.

The projector's light weight (just under 7 pounds) and portability make it a good match for golf simulation. I found it easy to position the projector on the floor and then use it on a table or even in another room without lugging it around like a massive brick.

I first had to figure out where to place it for the golf sim, though. As a short-throw projector, it should normally sit about 4 feet away from the screen. Since I wouldn’t be using actual golf clubs, I could set it on the floor in my windowless testing room; otherwise, I would have to mount it on the ceiling, away from swinging clubs. The projected image looked big enough that, when I started playing EA Sports PGA Tour, the players looked about as tall as they are in real life.

Photograph: John Brandon

I noticed Optoma offers an app to help with initial setup, but it’s a hassle to use. You have to install the app and sync over Bluetooth, but I found it was easier to just do the keystone adjustment with the included remote. (Also, Optoma did not include the required Bluetooth dongle even though it is normally part of the package.)

Tech.title: Border Wall Construction Threatens 6,000 Years of History on Private Lands
Tech.content:
Outrage has exploded over border infrastructure that recently began tearing up pristine desert landscapes in Big Bend National Park. But there’s a quieter battle taking place on private lands in Texas, where the US border wall is set to cut across some of North America's richest archaeological sites, digging up ancient indigenous artifacts and fracturing millennia-old rock art in its path.

The US Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection awarded billions of dollars in contracts this year toward the construction of a wall and other barriers in West Texas along a remote 500-plus-mile (800-plus-kilometer) riverfront expanse of the US-Mexico border that includes Big Bend National Park and other idyllic parklands.

Bipartisan backlash against border wall construction in the national park was swift, ultimately prompting DHS to scuttle plans for a 30-foot steel bollard wall, instead replacing it with miles of riverside vehicle barriers and 200-plus miles of road construction. Bulldozers began clearing along the Rio Grande corridor near Santa Elena Canyon on August 6.

Construction has since been paused in the park in response to lawsuits. But the agency is still planning to construct the wall, as well as a web of road construction, over mountains and across canyons outside the national park. That includes private property that ranchers and other landowners say have archeological sites worth protecting, too. And they’re concerned that construction of the wall will bifurcate their own land and damage archeological sites, many of which have yet to be fully studied.

Archeologist Bryon Schroeder has been digging on rancher Jeff Fort’s property for two years. Schroeder runs Sul Ross University’s Center for Big Bend Studies, a research program dedicated to studying the cultural, historical, and archeological legacy of the region. He removes 4 inches (10 centimeters) of sediment at a time, and his meticulous digs have uncovered pottery and melted adobe slick building material from as early as the year AD 800. He’s found turquoise, too, and marine shells, both signs of trade outside the region. Evidence shows the site is related to Paquimé, an UNESCO World Heritage site that’s 200 miles away in Mexico.

Schroeder’s dig site, Canta Recio, is directly in the path of the proposed wall. Some of it is set to be bulldozed over. If the wall is built, other parts of the site will also become effectively inaccessible.

Schroeder likens Canta Recio to how Egyptians set up shop along the Nile, surmising the site was settled four or five times between 800 and 1400 by groups who were likely drawn to fertile land afforded by routine floods. Of course, those floods also mean that groups were eventually forced to move on when the Rio Grande overtopped its banks, only for another group to eventually settle the area once the silt firmed up. A settlement, a flood, an exit, on repeat.

“There's some bigger, cooler sites up the river that are just insane,” Schroeder said. “They have so much pottery, they have Mesoamerican copper bells, they have turquoise. They have all sorts of crazy stuff.”

The paradox facing Schroeder and other archeologists: They can't fully measure what's at risk because many of the archeological sites exist on private ranches and have never been studied.

That means construction may erase history before anyone gets to record it. A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told WIRED that the agency is conducting environmental and cultural reviews to minimize impacts and balance operational needs with responsible land stewardship.

But previous studies haven’t stopped historically important sites from being sentenced to destruction. A 30-foot bollard wall is set to go right through the Polvo site, in Redford, Texas, which is home to a prehistoric village complete with burial ground dating back to the 1300s. The same site also has evidence of a Spanish mission that was built in the 1600s. Eagle Nest Canyon in Langtry, one of the most significant and intensively studied archeological sites in all of Texas, is also slated to see some form of barrier erected through it. That site includes the southernmost bison jump site in the US, where Native Americans hunted the animals en masse by funneling them over a cliff.

Tech.title: It Should Be Harder to Apply for a Job. No, Really
Tech.content:
Three years ago, Andrew Stockwell had his hiring routine down to a science.

As head of people for the software-buying company Vendr, Stockwell posted a listing, waited a few days, and then reviewed a few dozen applications—up to 100, if he was lucky. Recruiters identified other potential candidates, adding a few more applicants to the mix. Stockwell read résumés, conducted interviews, and passed along sterling candidates to hiring managers.

“It was really about finding that great talent, sussing out that talent, speaking with that talent, and identifying the best possible people,” Stockwell tells WIRED.

Sometime in the last year or so, Stockwell says, everything changed. The process started off the same way, but within a day or two, Stockwell wasn’t looking at 100 candidates. Instead, he was flooded with hundreds of applications. Sometimes, the incoming topped a thousand. A good chunk were “total bogus,” Stockwell says—fake candidates. Many more appeared to have been written using artificial intelligence, stretching the truth and making it difficult to distinguish one applicant from another. The sheer quantity was overwhelming. Stockwell says he found himself “paying my talent-acquisition professionals—who are high-paid, high-quality individuals—just to look through applications all day long.”

Stockwell is one of many recruitment professionals who believe looking for a job is fundamentally broken. In 2026, job hunting has become as easy as online shopping: AI can crank out tailored résumés and cover letters in seconds. Browser extensions can autofill applications, no human necessary. LinkedIn serves users dozens of jobs a day, many with the option to apply with “just a few clicks.”

“A year ago, every recruiter would tell me: We want to make it as easy as possible to apply for jobs,” offering candidates a “seamless experience,” Ophir Samson, the head of voice AI for Greenhouse, tells WIRED. Samson joined the recruiting platform earlier this year, when it acquired his startup, which used AI to conduct job interviews. “What they got was 2,000 applicants in 24 hours for a job. That is a shitty experience for everyone.”

Good applicants can’t stand out, while bad candidates slip through the cracks. Recruiters, Samson says, face the tortuous task of judging thousands of candidates, every single day. Instead of taking the time to search LinkedIn for dream employees, they spend hours in applicant tracking systems, tweaking filters to try to determine whose applications are worth a 30-second skim.

Now, recruiters are telling Samson, “actually, we kind of want friction,” he says. “The friction is good. We want to make it harder.”

The desire to remove pain points in the application process makes sense: If the highest number of qualified candidates apply for a role, it stands to reason that a company can maximize the chances of finding the best possible fit. So for years, recruiters have posted on job boards and LinkedIn; they signed up for LinkedIn’s “Easy Apply” feature; they promised candidates a “one-click” application process. Post-pandemic, recruiters’ efforts to simplify the process went into superdrive, as employers struggled to fill open roles.

“Everyone was job hopping, because you literally could have three offers in an afternoon,” Jane Curran, the chief transformation officer at real estate giant JLL, tells WIRED. Now, “it is the polar opposite.”

Openings peaked at a record 12.3 million in March 2022, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, followed by two years of decline. Since mid-2024, openings have hovered at around 7 million, give or take 500,000.

But as the number of job openings contracted, the barriers to entry for applying declined even further. AI—which entered the mainstream in late 2022 with the public release of ChatGPT—allows applicants to rewrite résumés and track new postings almost instantaneously. Companies like JobAssist, Sonara, and Ladder’s Apply4Me promise applicants that their technology will handle all the busy work of applying for jobs, by submitting “10x as many applications with less effort than one manual application.” If you wanted to, you could apply for dozens of jobs a day.

Tech.title: Americans Want to Know When Their Healthcare Providers Use AI
Tech.content:
AI chatbots are being used in healthcare, both in and out of the doctor’s office, more than ever before. Patient and medical providers alike are turning to AI for treatments and diagnoses, but transparency remains a key concern, a new survey by Pew Research Center shows.

A poll of 3,488 US adults conducted between June 22 and June 28 found that a quarter of respondents use chatbots to diagnose symptoms. Those turning to chatbots for health mainly cite convenience and affordability as their motive. Patients also use AI chatbots to find information quickly and at no cost, better understand a doctor’s diagnosis, interpret lab results and decide whether to seek in-person care.

Of these survey participants, almost half (47%) say the health information generated by the chatbot was “extremely” helpful, and 48% said the information was “somewhat” helpful. Only 5% said the results were not too helpful or not at all helpful.

AI chatbots work by simulating a conversation between two parties and responding to your prompts or inputs using the massive amounts of information the models were trained on. Many people appreciate the convenience they offer, as chatbots are available 24/7 and can often be accessed for free and sometimes without an account. Chatbots, however, are known to “hallucinate,” or generate false information in their responses, which can be particularly dangerous or alarming when your personal health is in question. Among other issues, they’re trained to produce a probable answer, not necessarily one grounded in truth, and they’re likely to sound particularly confident about that answer.

But generative artificial intelligence is also showing up at the doctor’s office — and Pew found that Americans have greater concerns about its use there.

Read also: ChatGPT Health Will See You Now, and It’s a Big Step Forward for Medical Queries

When doctors turn to chatbots

While recent numbers show that about one in three US adults have used chatbots for health-related questions, medical providers are also increasingly turning to AI in the office for note-taking, interpreting exams and more.

While views on AI use in doctors’ offices vary, one factor remains of critical concern to patients: transparency.

Of those surveyed, 72% say it is “extremely or very important” for their medical provider to disclose any use of AI. The survey also found that a vast majority of people (eight in 10) want to be told if AI is being used directly for care or medical decisions, such as diagnoses and the analysis of scans, X-rays and lab results. AI is frequently used for triage purposes — and has even been shown to outperform human ER doctors — as well as to complete clinical tasks more quickly. For instance, AI has been used effectively to reduce the window of X-ray interpretations from 11.2 to 2.7 days.

Although Americans want advance notice when AI is used in their healthcare, nearly half (47%) are unsure whether it has ever played a role in their treatment, underscoring limited awareness of when, where and how the technology is used.

Americans are not fully comfortable with AI

The survey shows that Americans may find AI chatbots convenient, but not entirely trustworthy.

Views are mixed on sharing personal health histories and diagnoses with AI. Among those surveyed, 29% say they are extremely or very comfortable sharing health information with chatbots, while 26% say they are uncomfortable doing so.

The findings suggest that although AI is increasingly used for health information and care, public confidence and understanding have not kept pace with its adoption.

Tech.title: Foldable iPhone Ultra, iPhone 18 Pro and Other Phones We Expect to Launch in 2026
Tech.content:
While this year started with a few iterative phone launches, the last couple of months have taken us back into the exciting phones territory. From the all-new wide Galaxy Z Fold 8 to a software-centric Pixel 11 upgrade, we’re fresh off the flagship launch cycle from Samsung and Google. Now, it’s time for Apple to take the stage. We’re likely just a couple of weeks away from the next-generation iPhones.

However, the ongoing RAM shortage and growing competition in generative AI are making it harder for phone-makers to deliver bold designs and features that are both useful and innovative without pushing prices too high. This could lead Apple to shake things up with its iPhone 18 lineup. While the long-rumored foldable iPhone Ultra is tipped to debut next month, the base iPhone 18 model might launch early next year.

It’s already the end of August, but there’s a lot to look forward to in the coming months. Apart from Apple, there are more high-end phones coming out of China. While the Galaxy Z TriFold and Oppo Find N6 took a radical approach to design, the Ultra models from Vivo, Oppo and Xiaomi took mobile photography to the next level. And we might see a few high-end features trickle down to their Pro siblings in the upcoming months.

The bottom line? 2026 is far from over, and some of the most impressive phones have yet to be revealed.

Phones released in 2026 so far

Apple

The iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max marked the return of vibrant colors to Apple’s highest-end iPhones. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

A split iPhone 18 launch strategy

Apple introduced a slew of upgrades with the iPhone 17 line — an 18-megapixel selfie shooter, upgraded rear camera optics, thermal cooling on the Pro variants, among other updates. It also added the thin iPhone Air to the lineup. This year, the Cupertino company could shake up its iPhone launch timeline.

For years, Apple has continued to announce the base iPhone model alongside its Pro siblings, while also experimenting with Mini, Plus and Air variants. This could change in 2026. According to a report from The Information and Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, the Cupertino-based company may push the launch of the vanilla iPhone 18 to early 2027 in a bid to make space for the iPhone Fold.

Apple could still announce multiple iPhone models in September 2026, but the lineup and timing would look slightly different. Next month, we could see the launch of the next-gen. iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max in new colors and the all-new iPhone Fold (or iPhone Ultra). But the standard iPhone 18 is tipped to be released alongside the iPhone 18E in March 2027.

The new Apple iPhone launch cycle might be:

March 2026: iPhone 17E

September 2026: iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and iPhone Fold

March 2027: iPhone 18, iPhone 18E and iPhone Air 2

September 2027: iPhone Air 3, iPhone 19 Pro/Pro Max and iPhone 20 (named to honor the 20th anniversary of the original iPhone’s 2007 debut)

Since the standard iPhone 18 model is rumored to be released in 2027, let’s focus on the iPhone variants that are more likely to be launched this year.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

CNET’s Jeffrey Hazelwood created these custom renders of what an iPhone 18 Pro might look like in purple, coffee and burgundy. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

The iPhone 18 Pro models are expected to have the same design language as the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max but be available in new colors. Apple is said to be considering three color options to replace 2025’s cosmic orange: coffee, purple and burgundy.

I’d love a burgundy or coffee-brown iPhone 18 Pro. I’m more intrigued by the latter, thanks to CNET Jeffrey Hazelwood’s mock-ups of the iPhone 18 Pro in purple, coffee and burgundy, which you can see above.

Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to have the same 6.3-inch and 6.9-inch displays, respectively, as the current models. However, Apple is rumored to opt for an under-display Face ID True Depth camera to make the Dynamic Island smaller.

There have also been rumors about the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, including an under-display Face ID, alongside a punch-hole cutout for the selfie shooter, which is common on Android phones. According to the same report from The Information cited above, the iPhone 18 Pro duo’s displays will have a small hole in the top-left corner to house the front-facing camera. So, we shouldn’t expect a full-screen display with an under-display camera.

I’ve used phones with under-display cameras (RedMagic 10 Pro and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 5), and while I love having a full-screen experience, I look smudgy on video calls and selfies with these cameras. No phone manufacturer has figured out a way to retain photo quality while delivering a full-screen experience with an under-display camera.

If Apple can do that, I’d be pleasantly surprised. But it seems unlikely as current-gen iPhones launched with a new industry-leading 18-megapixel Center Stage camera on the front. I don’t think Apple would mess with that. I expect the same photo and video quality on the next iPhone.

Apple moved to a new camera plateau design with the iPhone 17 Pro lineup. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Moving to the rear optics, Apple is reportedly introducing a variable aperture lens on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. It might be irrelevant to most people, but for those who use their iPhones for photography, a variable aperture would offer more control over their photos. It would allow you to manually adjust the amount of light reaching the sensor and the depth of field on a subject.

This isn’t groundbreaking new technology. Samsung introduced it with the Galaxy S9 in 2018 but it remained ineffective due to the small sensor size and the fact that the aperture could only switch between two f-stops: f/1.5 and f/2.4.

Xiaomi and Huawei did a better job with their flagships in 2023. The Huawei Mate 50 Pro offered 10 aperture steps (f/1.4 to f/4.0), while the Xiaomi 13 Ultra has a dual-aperture design (f/1.9 and f/4.0) paired with a larger 1-inch-type image sensor.

Based on these examples, Apple will likely need to add a larger image sensor and more flexibility with aperture control to make it actually useful. It could be a godsend to improve the iPhone’s portrait mode, which trails behind the likes of current Vivo, Oppo and Xiaomi phones.

The iPhone 18 Pro is also rumored to get a new three-layer stacked image sensor developed by Samsung. For years, Sony has supplied the image sensors for the iPhone. Samsung’s sensor could reduce noise in images, improve the dynamic range and make the iPhone’s camera more responsive.

The iPhone 18 Pro series is expected to be powered by the A20 Pro chipset, built on TSMC’s 2nm process. It could have architectural changes, such as having RAM integrated directly onto the same wafer as the CPU, GPU and neural engine, instead of it being adjacent to the chip and connected via an interposer. It could allow for 30% better efficiency and 15% faster performance than the A19 chips. The next iPhones may also use Apple’s next-generation C2 modem chip for enhanced wireless connectivity.

The foldable iPhone Ultra

This is a mock-up of what a possible iPhone Fold might look like, according to CNET designer Jeffrey Hazelwood. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

There are conflicting rumors about the launch timeline of Apple’s foldable iPhone. Some say it’ll be released alongside the iPhone 18 Pro series this year, while a report from The Elec claims that the launch could be delayed to 2027. It’s worth noting that rumors of Apple’s book-style foldable iPhone date back to 2019. However, the recentiOS 27 Developer Beta‘s app resizability feature hints at a 2026 launch timeline.

Apple’s first folding phone is likely to be a book-style foldable, like the Galaxy Z Fold, rather than a clamshell flip phone. It’ll have a smaller outer display and a wider folding display — like the first-gen Google Pixel Fold, per Kuo. I used the Oppo Find N in 2022, which had a similar passport-size form factor. While Oppo’s foldable is better for watching videos, it didn’t offer the best experience for browsing the web.

One of the best aspects of the first Pixel Fold was its passport book-style design and size. James Martin/CNET

If Apple can find the middle ground between the Pixel Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 7, the iPhone Fold could be an enticing choice. It is rumored to include a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.8-inch display when unfolded.

According to Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, the first folding iPhone is expected to measure 4.5mm thick when unfolded. For context, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7 measures 4.2mm, while the Huawei Mate XT (the tri-fold) is 3.6mm thick when fully opened.

In his blog, Kuo gave more clarity on the expected release date and shipment delays. He says that the development of the foldable iPhone “is behind earlier expectations.” The new Apple iPhone is still on track to be launched in 2026 but “smooth shipments may not occur until 2027.”

Here’s a mock-up of the Galaxy Z Fold with iPadOS overlayed on top of the screen. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

A report from The Elec (via DigiTimes) says that Apple will use ultra-thin glass for its first foldable iPhone. It could have a hole-punch selfie shooter on the cover screen and an under-display camera behind the inner screen. It’ll likely lack Face ID and rely on Touch ID for biometric authentication.

Kuo also reported that the first Apple foldable will minimize the crease by using a combination of titanium, stainless steel and liquid metal for the hinge. It’s also tipped to use titanium for its frame and aluminum in other areas. The foldable iPhone is rumored to house a 48-megapixel primary camera alongside a 48-megapixel ultrawide-angle sensor. Apple might not give it a telephoto camera.

Recently, longtime Apple leaker Sonny Dickson shared what appear to be 3D CAD renderings of the rumored device. These renderings align with a separate CAD leak from December published by GSMArena. They show a book-style foldable iPhone with a wide aspect ratio — giving us an iPad Mini-size display. It appears to be a hybrid of the iPhone 17 Pro and the iPhone Air, with a dual-tone look and a pill-shaped camera module at the top. The upcoming iPhone Fold looks like a passport-sized phone.

Another Mark Gurman report from Bloomberg revealed new information about how Apple will tweak iOS for its new iPhone. The iPhone Fold is likely to run iOS 27, which is focused on smarter Siri and OS stability. While the company didn’t detail any multiwindow or split-screen support at WWDC 26, it told developers to move away from designing apps for specific devices and fixed orientations at the Platforms State of the Union. They’re advised to target “a dynamic range of sizes and aspect ratios,” which could hint at dynamic app scalability on iPhone Ultra’s expansive inner screen.

The foldable iPhone is said to cost between $1,800 and $2,500. While earlier rumors suggested the latter price, recent rumors have said that the folding iPhone will cost the same as the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7 and Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold.

Samsung

The Galaxy S25 Ultra debuted in January 2025. Josh Steinbauer/CNET

Samsung has seemingly announced all its flagship phones for the year. It started with a trifold phone and carried forward that innovative energy to its mainstream foldable phones. The Korea-based phone-maker has had its ups and downs in 2026, but it has delivered some amazing devices.

In January, it announced the Galaxy Z TriFold, which was extremely limited in availability. The Huawei Mate XT competitor opted for a different folding design; this compromised its usability, but the overall tablet-in-pocket design was terrific nonetheless. The following month, Samsung launched the Galaxy S26 series with forgettable upgrades to the S26 and S26 Plus, but added a unique Privacy Display feature on its top-of-the-line Ultra model. I wish it had added the same privacy capability on the Folds this year. While that didn’t happen, it launched an all-new wide Galaxy Z Fold 8 in July, which has been my favorite folding phone of the year. The new Flip 8 and Fold 8 Ultra are fine in their own ways, but the Fold 8 is the best combination of flip pocket-ability and fold usability.

While we’re unlikely to get any more flagship phones from Samsung this year, the Galaxy S27 series is reportedly bracing for a redesign. According to leakers Ice Universe, Sonny Dickson and Max Jambor, the Galaxy S27 series could adopt a camera bar design similar to the iPhone 17 Pro series.

Google

Google Pixel 11 Pro brings software-led changes. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Google’s Pixel 11 series arrived in August, focusing on new software features and a bigger camera sensor on the Pixel 11 Pro. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold also got a slightly thinner and lighter design over last year’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold. While a lot of the hardware remained similar to last year’s Pixel 10 series, many of the small revisions added up to noticeable improvements, including faster 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging using the phones’ PixelSnap magnets and the 40% slimmer camera bar on the Pixel 11 over the Pixel 10.

The 2026 Google Pixel lineup is led by useful smart features. CNET’s Mike Sorrentino put it best in his review: “Pixel-specific features like Live Translate are jaw-dropping and show the lengths Google has gone to make accessibility a priority.” The underwhelming HiLight LED feature and $100 price hike across the lineup might sting, but each new Pixel phone can stand its own.

Where is OnePlus?

OnePlus has already announced its OnePlus 13 successor: the OnePlus 15. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Unfortunately, we won’t get any more OnePlus flagships in the US. In July, the company confirmed that it’ll no longer operate in North America or Europe, and won’t launch any further phones in the regions following 2025’s OnePlus 15. It had already merged some of its operations with its parent company Oppo in 2021, but all of its operations will now fall under the Oppo brand. OnePlus will continue to operate in China and India, but it’s unlikely to announce a top-end flagship phone this year.

Xiaomi’s first-ever IFA entry

Ahead of the expected Apple event in September, Xiaomi could announce a new foldable phone in the first week of September. At its Xiaomi 17T phone launch event in May 2026, the company confirmed it will make its first-ever appearance at the IFA Berlin trade show.

According to recent rumors, Xiaomi could use this opportunity to announce its new folding phone, which could differ from its current generation of flip phones and book-style foldables.

As per a Weibo post by Beginners Review, the internal HyperOS prototype UI design is believed to be of a wide-screen folding phone. While it could also be a tablet, Xiaomi’s first-ever presence at IFA is likely about an all-new shape. It could join the likes of Huawei, Apple and Samsung in developing a passport-like folding phone.

Tech.title: Your Internet Bill Might be Booby Trapped. Here’s What to Do
Tech.content:
Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty Images

From comparing the best internet providers in your area to understanding your actual speed needs, we’ve spent years here at CNET covering the best ways to lower the cost of home internet. But how did our internet bills get so high in the first place?

It wasn’t an accident, that’s for sure. According to a recent CNET survey, over 63% of adults in the US saw their internet prices increase year over year. That’s what happens when the wide majority of plans come with a flashy promotional rate packed with fine print designed to balloon your bill in the long run.

Internet service providers don’t always make it easy to avoid unpleasant billing surprises like those, but we can help. Keep reading for a full guide to common home internet pricing traps and the best ways to shield your budget from them.

This article was made possible in part by Xfinity. It was written and edited independently without partner oversight.

So… your internet bill doubled

Most of us have moved into a new home and needed to set up a fresh internet connection. Here’s how it usually goes: You try signing up online, but after a few clicks, you’re directed to give the company a call instead. So, you hop on the phone with a plan in mind, but pretty soon, the customer service representative starts selling you on a faster plan.

The pitch sounds pretty good – zippy speeds, maybe a free streaming subscription or two to go with them and, to top it all off, a discounted promotional rate on your monthly bill. You decide to go for it. Boom, your home internet is taken care of, your speeds are nice and fast, and you think you scored a sweet deal in the process. Wrong.

A year passes, and you notice your monthly bill has doubled in price. Sound familiar?

You call your internet provider, and the voice on the other end explains that your price increased because your promotional rate expired. So now, you’ll be paying a higher rate. Oh, and remember those free streaming services that were bundled in? Those were only included during the promotional period. At this point, the customer service rep might even try to offer you another promotional plan – for one year – followed by yet another, even bigger price increase.

That’s just one example of a common home internet pricing trap, and it’s the kind of thing that causes people to pay far more than they need to for their home internet service. The good news is that you don’t have to fall for schemes like these. You just have to know how to spot them.

Feodora Chiosea/Getty images

What are pricing traps?

Pricing traps are essentially tactics businesses use to lure customers into paying more for something. For instance, your ISP will happily talk you into paying more for a faster plan with speeds your home doesn’t always need. Others will insist that the best value only comes once you’ve bundled your home internet with a mobile or TV package you might not have been interested in to begin with. In either case, the end result is that you’re paying more than you probably would have if you had never talked to a salesperson at all.

Promotional rates are a favorite of the ISP industry, and they’re also the most common home internet pricing trap. Those rates look tempting at a glance, but they amount to little more than mousetrap cheese if the promotional period is short. Once that promo period ends, the trap is sprung, and you’re stuck paying more.

Here are all of the most common techniques that ISPs use to lure you into paying more:

The most common internet pricing traps

The trap How to avoid it Promotional pricing Your provider lures you in with a discounted rate for the first year. After year one, your bill shoots up. Consider multiyear price lock offers that cost less in the long run. If none are available, be sure to do the math on the full cost of any contract before signing it Perks and freebies The provider offers free devices, streaming subscriptions, or gift cards to lure you into signing up for an expensive plan with speeds you don’t actually need Understand how much speed your home actually needs before signing up. Don’t upgrade to a faster plan just because the incentives are tempting Terms of service & hidden fees

Sometimes, the ISP will tuck away additional costs, hidden in the terms of service. These can include installation charges, surprise equipment fees, activation charges or fees if you decline auto pay. Always check the FCC-required broadband facts label first. These are your nutrition labels for each plan, along with any potential surprise fees. If the facts label doesn’t tell you when the promotional period ends or what your cost will be after – that’s a red flag. Data caps and overage fees Some internet plans include a data cap. Once you’ve used more data than it allows in a month, your speeds plummet or, worse, you’re charged overage fees Always check the broadband facts label to see whether your plan includes these fees. By law, ISPs must present access to the broadband label before the point of sale (online). If you can’t find it – that’s a red flag, too. Bundling home internet with a mobile or TV service Your ISP offers to bundle your home internet with a mobile or TV package, or with streaming add-ons. The upfront savings are a mask for steep price increases down the line Make certain that you understand any potential pricing increases before you sign a long-term contract. If it’s a good deal now and a bad deal later, it’s a bad deal overall.

How to protect yourself from internet providers’ pricing traps

According to CNET’s most recent analysis, the average monthly cost for home internet in the US was $73. That’s a little under $900 per year for home internet. Let’s say that’s what you’re paying, but then a pricing trap adds $30 to your monthly bill. Now, you’re spending more than $1,200 per year – and that will continue until you do something about it.

In other words, it’s well worth it to steer clear of those price traps from the get-go. Here are our top recommendations on how to do just that.

FCC

Broadband labels: Check plan type, pricing details and contract terms

The Federal Communications Commission now requires ISPs to display clear details about the prices, speeds and terms of each of its plans on “Broadband Facts” labels, inspired by the classic nutrition facts labels found on food packaging. The facts labels must be placed before the point of sale, not after. The idea is the same: consumers deserve to know the critical facts about what they’re buying without marketing mumbo jumbo or other obfuscation.

These details might look a little intimidating at first, but don’t be spooked. They’re here to help. Up top, you’ll find essential info about the plan in question, including speeds, pricing details and the length of the contract. Crucially, the label will make clear if you’ll be paying a promotional price and, if so, how long it lasts and what you’ll be paying afterward. If trap pricing is in play, this is the easiest place to spot it.

Besides prices, these broadband labels will clarify the exact download and upload speeds each plan offers. They also indicate if the plan comes with unlimited data or if there’s a monthly data cap you should be aware of.

FCC/Viva Tung/CNET

Don’t take the bait, stick to your script

Former CNET broadband reporter Cierra Noffke has had her fair share of experiences dealing with pricing traps from internet providers. When signing up for a 300-megabits-per-second plan from her internet provider, a persuasive and persistent customer service representative tried to get her to switch to a 500 Mbps or gigabit plan instead.

“She was making me second-guess myself,” Noffke said.

In the end, Noffke and her partner stuck to their guns. 300 Mbps was more than enough for their needs, thank you very much. The key? They understood their typical home internet usage before making the call.

“You really need to have your script and just write down everything that you’re going to say and just be strong with that,” Noffke wrote.

Call your ISP and negotiate your price

Former CNET staffer Danni Santana told me he first signed up for Optimum in 2018. He was paying about $45 a month for speeds of 300Mbps, but said he noticed that his monthly bill typically increased by $5 to $10 each year. Santana started a new yearly tradition of his own: calling Optimum to let them know he would be switching providers.

“You should always check your recurring bills,” Santana said.

A customer service representative is likely motivated to keep you as a customer, and that gives you leverage to negotiate. In Santana’s case, he was able to downgrade his plan to the speed and price he wanted while still keeping his HBO Max subscription.

Explore low-cost internet options or longer price locks

This might seem obvious, but one way to lower your internet bill is to switch to a cheaper provider. Most of the major ISPs offer entry-level plans at a good value.

You’ll still need to watch out for those pesky promotional price increases, but we’re also seeing a growing number of plans that promise to lock your price in for multiple years. For instance, Xfinity now offers customers a five-year price guarantee for all plans. You’ll pay more per month than you would with other promotional offers, but unlike with those discounted rates, your bill won’t shoot up after a year.

ISPs that offer long-term price locks

Provider Connection type Promo / Price lock details Xfinity (Comcast) Cable 5-year price lock available Kinetic FIber Fiber 2-3 year price lock available T-Mobile 5G 5G Home Internet 5-year price lock available Verizon 5G 5G Home Internet 3-5 year price lock available Verizon Fios Fiber 3-5 year price lock available Optimum (Altice) Cable / Fiber 5-year price lock available Mediacom Cable 2-3 year price lock available Breezeline Cable 2,3 or 5-year price lock available WOW! Cable/Fiber Price for life offer

Some providers still offer cheaper internet rates to qualifying low-income households. Here are some of the most widely available discount plans in the country:

Xfinity (Comcast): Offers Internet Essentials ($9.95 a month for 50 Mbps). Optimum (Altice): Offers Optimum Advantage ($15 a month for 100 Mbps). Sparklight (Cable One): Offers Economy Internet ($15 a month). Spectrum (Charter): Offers Spectrum Internet Assist ($20 a month). AT&T Internet: Offers Access from AT&T ($30 a month for 100 Mbps). Cox Communications: Offers ConnectAssist / Connect2Compete ($30 a month). Mediacom: Offers Connect2Compete ($9.95 a month for families). Frontier: Offers Frontier Fundamental Internet (at a Lifeline rate). Verizon Fios / 5G: Offers Verizon Forward (Up to $30 a month off home internet).

ISPs that don’t provide a standalone low-income plan usually accept or apply the standard $9.25 Federal Lifeline monthly credit or bill waivers to existing tiers. If you think your home qualifies for the discount, it’s worth asking your provider about it.

Is too much internet speed a thing?

Absolutely. In fact, paying more for speeds you don’t actually need might be the biggest pricing trap of them all.

The FCC uses the word “broadband” as a blanket term for high-speed internet. The specific speeds that meet the definition: download speeds of at least 100Mbps and upload speeds of at least 20Mbps. Those speeds are a good starting point for most homes, fast enough to handle everyday browsing, streaming in 4K, video calls and gaming online.

If your home is large and there’s a lot of ground for the Wi-Fi to cover, you might want something faster, as wireless speeds will drop over Wi-Fi the farther you are from your router. You also might want a faster plan if you’ll be sharing the connection with multiple roommates or family members. Still, even in circumstances like those, anything more than a modest speed upgrade might be overkill.

The most noticeable performance improvements will come from upgrading to a plan with faster upload speeds (particularly for video calls, file transfers and online gaming), or from upgrading to a better type of internet connection altogether. For instance, if you’re a cable subscriber but fiber internet is available in your area, then you should consider switching, as fiber plans offer better reliability along with upload speeds that are just as fast as the download speeds.

Activity Usage required Our recommended speed Email 1Mbps 1Mbps Web browsing 3 to 5Mbps 5 to 10Mbps Social media 3 to 5Mbps 10Mbps Video calls 3 to 5Mbps 10 to 20Mbps HD streaming 5 to 10Mbps 10 to 20Mbps Online gaming 3 to 6Mbps 25 to 35Mbps 4K streaming 25Mbps 35Mbps

To learn more, read our guide on how much speed your household needs.

What’s the bottom line on internet pricing traps?

There’s no need to settle for paying too much for your home internet connection. Your best bet to avoid these broadband pricing traps is to do some research before signing up and stay vigilant when you hear these promotional offers from ISPs. Remember, a provider might offer enticing incentives upfront, but it’s essential to understand what you’ll be paying after those promotions expire.

If you’ve already gotten yourself stuck in a pricing trap, don’t give up hope. Call your provider to see if you can negotiate a new plan with a lower rate. If they won’t budge, call the competition and switch. Whatever you do, stay patient, persistent and polite.
